attacks.claim: On upstream 429 the handler retries once with no retry budget, no concurrency cap, and no shared backoff, and the retry bypasses the tenant bucket. Under saturation this doubles upstream calls and holds each client request open for up to 5s, so load and in-flight memory grow when upstream is already throttling.

attacks.claim: The retry path has no timeout bound. The first call, the sleep, and the second call can each block, so worst-case latency is roughly two upstream timeouts plus 5s. The diff sets no timeout on either call.

attacks.claim: The retry is designed to fail whenever upstream's Retry-After exceeds 5s. The code caps the wait and retries anyway, so those requests add 5s of latency and one extra upstream call for a request that will almost certainly get another 429.
attacks.evidence: "honoring its Retry-After capped at 5s" with MAX_UPSTREAM_RETRY_MS = 5_000 and no check that the capped wait is long enough to succeed

attacks.claim: The 20 rps / burst 40 default and the upstream retry take effect for all ~120 tenants on deploy, with no feature flag, kill switch, shadow mode, or staged enablement. Tenants whose legitimate traffic exceeds 20 rps start receiving 429s immediately, and the only rollback is a redeploy.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: no feature flag, kill switch, dry-run, or staged rollout. "limits from tenant config, default 20 rps / burst 40"

attacks.claim: Date.now can step backward. A negative elapsed time reduces tokens, and Math.min clamps only the upper bound, so tokens can go negative and lock the tenant out for a period proportional to the step size. The bucket recovers as time passes, so this is bounded rather than permanent. A monotonic clock would avoid it.
attacks.evidence: constructor(private now: () => number = Date.now) {} ... const elapsedSec = (nowMs - b.updatedMs) / 1000; b.tokens = Math.min(limits.burst, b.tokens + elapsedSec * limits.ratePerSec);

attacks.claim: The aggregate cap is unverified. Per-tenant 20 rps across ~120 tenants allows about 2400 rps total, and nothing shows that fits upstream capacity or quota. The per-tenant cap stops one tenant from starving others, but it does not stop the combined load from producing upstream 429s.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: any upstream capacity or quota figure. "default 20 rps / burst 40"

attacks.claim: keyFingerprint is an unsalted, truncated SHA-256 of the raw tenant API key, logged on every denial. It is a stable identifier derived from a secret. A keyed HMAC or the tenant id would be safer, and the log retention and access policy for this field is not addressed.

An info-level log line is written for every rejected request, so log volume grows linearly with offending traffic. A tenant at 400 rps produces 400 lines per second, which can drown logging and I/O during abuse.
attacks.evidence: req.log.info({ tenant: tenant.id, key: keyFingerprint(tenant.apiKey), waitMs }, "tenant rate limited");

attacks.claim: retryAfterMs parses only delta-seconds. An HTTP-date Retry-After yields NaN and silently falls back to 1s, so the upstream's requested wait is ignored without any log or test.
attacks.evidence:

attacks.claim: The tenant-limit Retry-After is rounded up to whole seconds. A tenant that needs about 50ms to recover is told to wait a full second, so well-behaved clients back off about 20x longer than necessary.
A zero or invalid ratePerSec from config divides by zero. waitMs becomes Infinity and the Retry-After header is set to the invalid string 'Infinity'. Limits are not validated at the point of use.

LRU eviction resets an evicted tenant's bucket to full burst. Idle-then-returning or churned tenants regain full burst, which defeats the limit once more than 10k tenants are active. The boundary is neither documented nor tested. It is not reached at ~120 tenants.
attacks.evidence: private buckets = new LRUCache<string, Bucket>({ max: 10_000 }); ... ?? { tokens: limits.burst, updatedMs: nowMs };

attacks.claim: Observability covers only denials. Admitted requests, retry outcomes, and pass-through second 429s produce no metric or log, so ops cannot alert on tenant starvation or retry storms, even though the PR says rate-limit decisions are logged.
attacks.evidence: req.log.info({ tenant: tenant.id, key: keyFingerprint(tenant.apiKey), waitMs }, "tenant rate limited");

attacks.claim: The gateway's own 429 and the passed-through upstream 429 share a status code. The gateway's error type is a free-text 'rate_limited' string, so clients cannot reliably tell which layer throttled them.
attacks.evidence: .send({ error: { type: "rate_limited", message: "tenant rate limit exceeded" } });
